The Gospels Sans Jesus

Fabrizio de André’s La buona novella

Filed under: Blog
18/x/2026 Tagged as:
  • review
La buona novella tracklist:
  1. Laudate dominum (‘Praise the Lord’)
  2. L’infanzia di Maria (‘Mary’s Childhood’)
  3. Il ritorno di Giuseppe (‘Joseph’s Return’)
  4. Il sogno di Maria (‘Mary’s Dream’)
  5. Ave Maria
  6. Maria nella bottega d’un falegname (‘Mary in a Carpenter’s Workshop’)
  7. Via della croce (‘Via Crucis’)
  8. Tre madri (‘Three Mothers’)
  9. Il testamento di Tito (‘Titus’s Will’)
  10. Laudate hominem (‘Praise the Man’)

Italy has a proud tradition of singer-songwriters, in Italian called cantautori (a pormanteau of cantatore ‘singer’ and autore ‘author’). Many consider the best representative of this tradition to be Fabrizio de André, known by the nickname Faber. The word faber (from Latin ‘smith; maker; artisan’) is a reference to de André’s favourite brand of pencils, Faber-Castelli, but is also a reference to his first name (Fabrizio sounds similar to the Italian fabbro ‘smith’) and to his status as a poet (via the metaphor Poet as Maker; see Andrew Hurley’s note to “The Maker” in his translations of Borges’s Collected Fictions). In fact, while some of his songs are very musically interesting, his melodies are for the most part very simple and what makes them so beautiful are his poetic texts.

After the 1968 student revolutions, while his contemporaries write songs and release albums celebrating or in some way commenting on them, de André begins work on an album retelling Jesus’s life.[1] He ultimately releases it in 1969 with the title La buona novella (‘The Good News’), a literal translation of the Greek εὐαγγέλιον (evangelion, ‘good news; Gospel’).

While he wasn’t an atheist, De André wasn’t exactly a Christian. Many of his songs, such as “Si chiamava Gesù” (‘His Name Was Jesus’), refer to his disbelief in Jesus being the son of God:

Non intendo cantare la gloria
Né invocare la grazia e il perdono
Di chi penso non fu altri che un uomo
Come dio passato alla storia…

I don’t mean to celebrate the glory
Or invoke the mercy and forgiveness
Of whom I think was a mere man
Who went down in history as a god…

His point of view on the New Testament is humanist. While he doesn’t believe in Jesus’s divinity, he sees him as a heroic figure who practiced what he preached—forgiveness and love of all men—to a truly superhuman extent. The song quoted above continues with these lines:

…Ma inumano è pur sempre l’amore
Di chi rantola senza rancore
Perdonando con l’ultima voce
Chi lo uccide fra le braccia d’una croce

…But nevertheless, inhuman is the love
Of him who groans [while dying] without resentment
Forgiving with his last breath
Those who kill him in the embrace of a cross

This conception of Jesus the Man as well as his deep reverence for him come to the fore in La buona novella. The narrative of the Gospels is inserted between the introductory “Laudate dominum” (from Latin ‘Praise the Lord’) and the closing “Laudate hominem” (‘Praise the Man’) and told through the lives of what are ordinarily considered secondary characters.

The story opens with “L’infanzia di Maria” (‘Mary’s Childhood’). In all four canonical gospels, Mary comes to us as a full-formed figure. Compared with the fact that she will give birth to the Redeemer, her past isn’t given a second thought. De André, on the other hand, dedicates considerable time to her tragic childhood as related by the apocryphal Gospel of James. As a child, Mary is taken away from her parents and made to grow up in a temple. Before she gets her first period, she is led out and presented in front of a crowd of male inhabitants. The choir’s initial compassionate address to Mary (‘the wind and the season have gone back to their games / but not with you, child kneeling in the temple’) turns into a jumbled mess of exclamations as the excited crowd scrutinises her appearance, falling over themselves in praising her face, her hair, her ‘flesh of paradise’—the tempo rises and makes you feel what Mary must have felt while being ogled by tens of her potential husbands.

Ultimately, a lottery draw assigns her to Joseph: to ‘fingers that are too dry / to cup a rose; / a heart too old / which is already resting.’ Mary’s youth (she is all of twelve years old when she’s married) is underscored in the following song, “Il ritorno di Giuseppe” (‘Joseph’s Return’), where Joseph brings her a wooden doll, so she can ‘return to those games / you had to abandon / when you were too young.’ After she learns that she will give birth to the Redeemer, there is the song “Ave Maria”, an ode dedicated to women who have had a similar fate to hers: who only got to be “femmine per poco / poi madri per sempre” (‘girls for a while / then mothers forever’).

Jesus’s birth is foretold in “Il sogno di Maria” (‘Mary’s Dream’), one of the most beautiful songs on the album. Mary dreams of being back in the temple of her childhood, when an angel comes and lets her fly away with him. The description of their flight reminds one of Shevchenko’s poem “The Dream”:

Poi d’improvviso mi sciolse le mani
E le mia braccia divennero ali
[…]
Volammo davvero sopra le case
Oltre i cancelli, gli orti, le strade
Poi scivolammo tra valli fiorite
Dove all’ulivo si abbraccia la vite

Then suddenly he untied my hands
And my arms became wings
[…]
We flew over the houses
Beyond the gates, gardens, streets
Then we floated between flowery hills
Where the olive tree and grapevine hug each other

When she wakes up from this state, which “forse era sogno / ma sonno non era” (‘might have been a dream / but not sleep’), an echo of the angel’s words still hangs in the air: “lo chiameranno figlio di Dio” (‘they’ll call him the son of God’). Repurposing the verb of the first line quoted above (“mi sciolse le mani”), the coda begins by saying that the already exhausted word “si sciolse in pianto” (‘melted into tears’).

“Via della croce” (‘Via Crucis’) neatly divides the album in two. Jesus’s torment is described only briefly; he is relegated to a side character as the narrative mostly focuses on the weeping widows and the terrified apostles. In the final verses, a description of the poor fluidly melts into an introduction of Titus and Dumachus, the two thieves crucified next to Jesus. For the narrative of “La buona novella,” they are more important and tragic than Jesus himself. In a way, they are closer to the Messiah presaged in Isaiah 53:3: unlike Christ, mourned by the multitude, they are the ones who are “despised and rejected of men”; they are “[men] of sorrows, and acquainted with grief.” The only ones to mourn the thieves are their mothers, and their grief is perhaps even more justified than Mary’s:

“Lascia a noi piangere un po’ più forte
Chi non risorgerà più dalla morte”

“Let us grieve a little bit louder
Those who won’t come back to life”

After the crucifiction, Jesus once more disappears. Instead we listen to Titus listing all ten comandments and trying to apply them to his own life. “Il testamento di Tito” (‘Titus’s Will’) with its compassion for the downtrodden inserts itself neatly into de André’s broader poetics:

Il quinto dice: Non devi rubare
E forse io l’ho rispettato
Vuotando in silenzio le tasche già gonfie
Di quelli che avevan rubato:
Ma io, senza legge, rubai in nome mio,
Quegli altri nel nome di Dio

The fifth [comandment] says that you shouldn’t steal
And maybe I did respect it
By quietly emptying the bulging pockets
Of those who had stolen:
But I, the outlaw, stole in my own name,
The others stole in the name of God

This sympathetic portrayal of the poor and of criminals is common in de André’s work. To take an example, compare the lines from ‘Titus’s Will’ with the final lines of “La città vecchia” (‘Old Town’), a song from a different album:

Se tu penserai, se giudicherai
Da buon borghese
Li condannerai a cinquemila anni
Più le spese
Ma se capirai, se li cercherai
Fino in fondo
Se non sono gigli, son pur sempre figli
Vittime di questo mondo

If you think and judge
Like a good bourgeois
You’ll sentence them to five thousand years
Plus compensation
But if you understand, if you look for them
All the way down
They may not be lilies, but they’re still sons
[And] victims of this world

Interestingly, prostitutes, one of the most common groups of ‘victims of this world’ which feature in many of de André’s other songs (think of “Via del campo” ‘The Field Road,’ “Bocca di rosa” ‘Rose Mouth’ or “La città vecchia”), are almost entirely absent here. The one exception is the description of the above-mentioned widows, who “ora soffron la pena / di chi perdonò a Maddalena” (‘now suffer the woe / of those who forgave Magdalene’). Except for this topic, however, the album contains all of the most important hallmarks of de André’s œuvre. What distinguishes it from the others (in my view) is its pathos and beautiful lyricism.

  1. He would later release an album that dealt with the student revolution: “Storia di un impiegato” (‘The Story of an Employee’). ↩︎
